body:
Found while fixing #2898.

## What happens

A flat Circular with several rings and a helix entry gets blocking `Crossing` warnings. Verification refuses the program. The post is held. The program is refused, not unsafe.

Reproduce with the job of #2898, with entry `Helix` and `helix_radius` 1:

- center [0,0], radius 10, tool EM-0600-4FL (25 mm flutes), stepover 2, stepdown 2
- top Z20, bottom Z0, clearance Z30, stock_to_leave 0

Generation reports pairs such as `feed moves 2 and 84 cross in XY at shared depth`. Each pair is a helix arc of ring k-1 and a helix arc of ring k at the same level.

## Cause

The Circular is ring-major: each ring runs its own level ladder, with its own entry at each level. Each helix passes through its ring's start, and its centre is one helix radius inward. When the stepover is two helix radii, the helix of ring k-1 touches the helix of ring k at the start of ring k. The two helices share one depth band. The crossing law (`crates/sim/src/verify/crossing.rs`) counts a touch as a crossing.

## What was tried

The fix branch of #2898 tried the pocket's z-major order for the flat mode (all rings at one plane). That removed the crossings. But the inner rings then started with an axial plunge that was not named, also under a ramp entry. Four ramp-entry tests went red. The branch dropped that approach (`docs/decisions/2898-circular-ring-links.md`).

## Expected

The helix entry of each later ring is placed so that it does not touch the helix of the ring before it, or the parameters are refused before generation with a named cause.

## Workaround

Use the plunge or the ramp entry, or one ring only.

body:
## What is missing

We want to post a CamCraft milling job as a conversational Heidenhain Klartext (`.H`) program. Our first target is a Fehlmann Picomax 55 with an iTNC 530 running NC software `340490-03`. CamCraft already writes Heidenhain DIN/ISO programs. Issue #3095 tests that post. Issue #2227 proposes a reader for Klartext files. This proposal concerns the writer.

## Proposed design

- Add one **Heidenhain Klartext** post alongside the DIN/ISO post. Keep the implementation, machine data, and test fixtures in CamCraft.
- Let the machine definition identify the installed control, its NC software, and its tool-change procedure. Record installed options when a supported feature needs them.
- Let the post select the documented syntax for that combination. For example, the Picomax needs a manual tool change with the quill at its physical change position. Other iTNC 530 machines can have a different tool changer.
- Start with one metric setup, three linear axes, stock bounds, preset selection, straight moves, plunges, and constant-height XY arcs. Refuse unsupported operations by name. Drilling cycles, tapping, probing, and tilted planes can have separate acceptance criteria later.

## What the local prototype shows

The prototype has one output implementation. It accepts the exact model and release above. Changing only the configured release to `340490-04` or `606425-04` makes it refuse the job before writing a file.

We ran two CamCraft programs on the Heidenhain iTNC 530 programming station, NC software `606425-04 SP20`. Its converter accepted all 41 blocks of a single-tool contour and all 63 blocks of a two-tool program. Test Run reached all three and five programmed stops, respectively. Both runs reached the end of the program without a logged NC error.

This supports those two programs on the station release. Acceptance on the physical `340490-03` installation remains open. Cycle 247 does not activate the preset during Test Run. Preset activation, quill clearance, and physical coolant operation still need checks on the machine. [HEIDENHAIN manuals for NC software 340 49x-03](https://content.heidenhain.de/doku/tnc_guide/html/en/index/1242135142456/1242135142480/1242135142485/1242135142485.html)

## Questions for the maintainers

1. Should the first release require an exact NC software match? When two releases document the same feature, what evidence should let them share the same output?
2. Which facts belong in the existing machine definition, and which should CamCraft maintain for each supported control? Tool-change behavior and supported cycle parameters are the first cases we would use to check that boundary.
3. Would one bounded draft PR suit the project? We propose to rework the local prototype after agreement, then submit the machine definition, post, golden output, and refusal tests together. We can split the machine-data changes first if that is easier to review. We would include the manual references, station results, and outstanding machine checks in the PR.

**Done means:** The maintainers record whether to proceed, the first supported scope, the evidence required, and the preferred PR split. We will wait for that decision before submitting code.

Suggested triage: `enhancement`, `needs-research`, `area:post`, `P8`, `effort:high`, `source:agent`.

body:
Research only. No code comes from this issue (AGENTS.md "needs-research").

**Why.** Many hobby router owners (WorkBee, Shapeoko, X-Carve, Onefinity, Laguna and Grizzly routers) use Vectric's **VCarve** or Delft Spline's **DeskProto**. Both are known for getting a first part cut quickly. One such user, MisterMaker on Discord (WorkBee with an Estlcam controller, #3038), never uses 3D CAM because building a 3D part from a 2D sketch is "too much of a hassle". Asked by the user (mkinney), 2026-11-20.

**Clean-room boundary** (same as #3045). The vendors' public material (feature pages, published manuals and tutorials, public videos) is used only as a checklist of which workflows and features hobby users expect. Never copied: wording, UI labels, parameter names, screen layouts, icons or dialog flows. Behaviour is specced from machining knowledge and our own design.

**Open questions**
1. **Typical first job.** What steps does a typical hobby job take in each tool: job and material setup, importing a 2D or 3D source, choosing toolpaths, the tool database, preview, saving G-code? Where does CamCraft take more steps or more knowledge today? Compare on 3 to 5 typical jobs: a sign, a V-carved name, an inlay, a 3D relief from an STL or image, a pocket and profile with tabs.
2. **Missing features.** Which hobby-router features do we lack or only half-cover? Candidates: V-carving (#1443), inlays, text and fonts, relief from an image or heightmap, tabs and bridges, ramps and lead-ins, "cut out" profiling, nesting (see #2395), toolpath templates, simple job wizards, machine and post pickers for common routers, simulated preview in wood colours.
3. **Defaults and presets.** Which defaults and starter presets would let a new router user get a safe first cut with no CAM knowledge? Router tool libraries (end mills, V-bits, ball noses) with conservative feeds, machine presets, material thickness and zero-point prompts.
4. **What not to copy.** Which of their simplifications would break our "never gouge, refuse with a reason" rules, and how do we keep the safety and still stay simple?
5. **Priorities.** A ranked list of sub-issues by how many router users each helps.

**Done means:** the questions answered in comments here and the sub-issues filed. Each sub-issue gets one P*, one effort:*, area:*, source:agent, a "Done means" line and "Part of #this". They are linked back, `needs-research` is dropped and this issue is closed.

Related: #3045 (conversational and no-model operations, the DXF/DWG route), #1443 (V-carve), #2395 (router tab), #1907 (Laguna and Grizzly routers), #3038 (WorkBee), #1880 (SVG import).

body:
A user who puts `camcraft-cli` on their PATH with a symlink (the usual way on macOS, where the binary is inside `CamCraft.app/Contents/MacOS/`) cannot post. MCP clients (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex, Cursor) are set up with such a path.

Reproduced on v0.24.0 (macOS, `camcraft-0.24.0-macos-universal.zip`), with one project:

| Started as | `process <project> -o out.nc` |
|---|---|
| `/Applications/CamCraft.app/Contents/MacOS/camcraft-cli` | rc 0, posted |
| a symlink to that file, in another folder | rc 1 |
| a copy of that file, in another folder | rc 1 |

The error of the symlink:

```
ERROR camcraft_app::posting::files: shipped posts file tormach.cps: no posts folder found - the program needs its assets/posts directory beside the executable (looked in: <folder of the symlink>/assets/posts)
camcraft-cli: post: built-in post Tormach PathPilot: no posts folder found ...
```

Cause: the posts folder is found beside the path of the started executable, without resolving the symlink to the real file.

Done means:
- A symlinked `camcraft-cli` finds the shipped posts (resolve the executable path with `std::fs::canonicalize` before the lookup), with a test.
- A plain copy still refuses with a clear message, as now. That message names the setting or environment variable to point at an assets folder, if there is one; otherwise it says to run the binary from the install folder or to use a symlink.
- The Windows and Linux layouts are checked the same way, and the result is recorded on this issue.

title: Viewport: the thick pick-outline highlight becomes a wedge that grows to the viewport edge at a low view angle

body: ## What happens When an operation's Geometry has a picked face, the viewport draws the face outline as a thick violet stroke with a dark halo (`pick_ink` -> `pick_highlight_mesh::paint_selected`, #1505). Seen from a low angle, the stroke becomes a wedge: a second violet line separates from the outline and grows wider toward the edge of the viewport, until it reaches the edge. - The wedge shows in all themes (dark and light). - The line width and the anti-aliasing do not change it. It shows at 1 pt with anti-aliasing Off on the #2958 branch. ## Where it comes from These three builds were compared at the same low view of the same project (a picked top face, Face operation): | Build | Result | |---|---| | v0.24.0 release | No wedge. Some halo segments disappear at some angles and zoom levels (see below). | | `main` at acd5b02d3 | Wedge | | `main` + #2989 | Wedge | The pick highlight was rewritten after v0.24.0, in PR #2256 (#2201: cached geometry, one batched mesh of stroke paths). Thus the wedge is a regression of that change. - A probe of `egui::epaint::Tessellator` with a thin, acute closed path does not extend past its points. Thus a miter at a sharp corner is probably not the cause. - A likely cause is the screen projection of the world points. `push_screen_polyline_runs` projects each point by itself (`interact::project_uv`). - A point behind the eye (`w <= 1e-6`) is dropped, and the run continues to the next point that projects. - A point just in front of the near plane projects to a very large screen position. - Neither case clips the segment at the near plane, so a run can connect two points that are not neighbours on the outline, or go to a point far off the screen. ## Related: the halo that disappears (also in v0.24.0) In v0.24.0, at some angles and zoom levels, parts of the thick stroke disappear, and only the thin depth-tested overlay line stays. The cause is the same projection: a segment with an end behind the eye is dropped. This is older than the wedge. ## Expected The thick pick outline follows the picked edges at each angle and zoom. A segment that crosses the near plane is clipped at the near plane. It is not dropped, and it is not connected to another part of the outline. ## Done means - Each segment of the selected-pick and hover highlights is clipped at the near plane in clip space before it is projected. - A run never joins two points that are not neighbours on the outline. - A test with a picked rectangle seen from a low angle, with a corner behind the eye: - Each stroke vertex stays within the stroke width of the projected (clipped) outline. - No segment of the outline is missing. Found during the test of #2958 (PR #2989). #2989 does not change this code. Proposed labels: `bug`, `P3`, `effort:medium`, `area:ui`, `source:agent`

## What happens

Indexed pocket operations can report a false shank collision with stock.
Found while building the catalog case for #2868, part of #2392.

The original blank spans X/Y -30..30 and Z0..70 mm.
The two side pockets use A+90/B0 and A-90/B0.
Their local top is 30 mm. Their local floor is 26 mm.
The 6 mm EM-0600-4FL cutter has a 15 mm flute length and no holder.
Generation reports shank collisions with uncut stock. Verification holds both operations.

## Cause

At upstream/main 58cb641ca, operation/generate.rs:205-206 computes stock_top_z in world coordinates.
At line 3638, the tilted branch initializes st_local with this world value minus origin Z.
Lines 3659-3666 only increase this value with projected box corners.
The correct local cap of 30 cannot replace the initial world value of 70.
The local shank bottom is about 41 mm at the pocket floor.
It clears the real stock cap of 30, but not the incorrect cap of 70.
The local verification therefore reports a collision.
stock_top_law.rs only rechecks RapidInStock warnings against the exact solids.
It does not recheck ShankHit warnings.

This differs from closed #903, which concerns the tilted band exclusion region.
The conservative box cap for an oblique face is a separate limitation.

## Expected

Compute the stock cap in the coordinate frame of the path under test.
Do not retain a world height as a lower bound for a local height.
Keep true shank collisions blocked.

## Done means

A pin with world Z70 and A+90/B0 uses the projected local stock cap of 30.
The A-90/B0 case has the same result.
A safe shank above the real stock cap passes. A real collision still blocks posting.

Priority: P3. A legal operation is refused; a smaller stock envelope avoids this cap error.
Effort: high. The fix changes collision verification and meets the safety floor.

body:
Found by the read-only review of PR #2985 (issue #2901). The PR records the gap in its decision file. This issue tracks it.

## What happens

PR #2985 adds the law `first_traverse_low`: the clearance plane of a milling operation must be above the top of the start stock and of each fixture, because the first traverse starts from an X/Y that is not known.

In a 3+2 frame the law does not read the box of the machine table (`crates/app/src/operation/first_traverse.rs:89-99`). The table box is a slab about 1,000,000 mm wide. Read along a tilted tool axis, its "top" is very large, and each indexed operation was refused. The PR thus skips the table when the frame is tilted. An upright frame still reads the table. The stock and the fixtures are read in each frame.

What stays without a check: the first traverse of each 3+2 operation against the machine table. A tilted clearance plane goes down toward the table on its low side, about 0.36 mm for each mm of travel at B 20 degrees. A real table can thus stand above the plane inside the travel of the machine. That is a collision that passes. Thus the priority is `P1`.

## Possible repair

Clip the table box to the travel of the machine (the machine file has the axis limits) before the corner reading. Then the law can read the table in a tilted frame.

## Done when

- A 3+2 operation whose clearance plane goes under the table top inside the machine travel is refused by name.
- The indexed example operations that post today still post.
- A machine file with no axis limits gives a defined result (a refusal or a note), not a silent pass.

Refs #2901, #2965

body:
The maintainer asked for this on 2026-11-20, after he saw that only one of the three runners works:

> The issue would need to not only split the post work into several "lanes" - it would also need to produce artifacts that gets collected and handed back for inspection. All the lanes could then be queued if we reduce the amount of runner but also run in parallell when we have more runners..

Now: `post-merge.yml` has one job, `gate`. It runs the whole batch tier (about 950 steps) on one runner. The runners `wopr` and `uma` have the label `camcraft-post-merge`. One of them works and the other waits. A run lasts about 40 minutes. The concurrency group `post-merge-main` allows one run at a time. A new push queues behind the running gate or cancels it.

Wanted:
- The batch tier is split into lanes. Each lane is one job of the workflow, for example a matrix over groups of test binaries, clippy, and the build.
- The lanes are independent. With three runners, three lanes run at the same time. With one runner, the lanes queue and give the same result as today.
- Each lane writes its logs and its result to an artifact (`gate-logs/` as `xtask gate` makes them). A final job collects all artifacts. It writes one verdict, with the red steps named, for the rolling issue `main is red (post-merge gate)`.
- A person or an agent can download the artifact of any lane and read the failure without a second run. The verdict names each lane, its runner, its time and its result.
- The report job (known defect #1611: skipped) is repaired or replaced as part of this work.

Open questions for the work:
- How `cargo xtask gate batch` splits into lanes: by a flag such as `--lane N/M`, or by named groups. The split must be deterministic, and each test binary must run in exactly one lane.
- How lanes share the build. Each runner builds the debug test binaries one time, or one job builds and uploads them. The compile cache (`sccache`) and the size of the artifacts matter here.
- How the lanes treat a push during a run (cancel all lanes, or finish and queue).

## What

A Slot with a width larger than the tool diameter leaves material in its two round ends. `verify` reports no problem, and the post is not blocked.

The work on the example case `2d/slots` (#2861, part of #2392) found this.

## How to reproduce

On `main` at `ab9955105`, run this script with a model `slots` (a 100 x 60 x 12 mm block, stock of the same size):

```js
cam.call("add_tool", { catalog: "EM-0600-4FL", holder: "none" });
cam.call("add_operation", {
  kind: "Slot", name: "Slot1", tool: "EM-0600-4FL", source: "slots",
  params: {
    a: [-25.0, 15.0], b: [25.0, 15.0], width: 10.0, stock_to_leave: 0.0,
    top_z: { reference: "top_of_stock", offset: 0.0 },
    bottom_z: { reference: "top_of_stock", offset: -6.0 },
    stepdown: 3.0, stepover: 2.0, feed: 600.0, plunge_feed: 150.0, climb: true
  }
});
cam.generate();
cam.verify();   // ok
```

## What the program does

The tool is 6 mm and the slot is 10 mm wide. The tool centre must stay in a stadium of 2 mm radius around the line `a -> b`. Each level posts three rows:

```
G01 X-25. Y13. Z9. F150
G01 X25. Y13. Z9. F600
G01 X27. Y15. Z9. F600
G01 X-27. Y15. Z9. F600
G01 X-25. Y17. Z9. F600
G01 X25. Y17. Z9. F600
```

The rows touch the round end only at their end points. The tool does not follow the arc between two row ends. The move between two rows is a straight line (a chord), not an arc.

## Measured

A point check of the 10 mm stadium against the tool centre path gives these results:

- The largest leftover is 0.86 mm, on the wall of each round end at 45 degrees, where no move joins two rows.
- The leftover is 0.59 mm at the two corners where a chord joins two rows.
- The total area that is not cut is about 8.9 mm2 for each level.

The straight walls are correct. The rows at `Y13` and `Y17` cut them to size.

## Expected

One of these:

- The Slot cuts its full outline. For example, the tool follows the two half circles of the tool centre stadium at each level.
- The operation reports the leftover as a warning that names the Slot and the largest leftover.

## Workaround

- Use a smaller `stepover`. The leftover becomes smaller, but it does not go to zero.
- Use a Trochoidal slot of the same width. Its last move is a half circle around `b`, and its entry is a full circle around `a`.

## Notes

- The row law is in `crates/motion/src/machining2d/slots.rs` (`SlotParams`: "each row reaches the round ends exactly as far as it can").
- The case `examples/catalog/2d/slots` shows the two programs side by side. A fix changes `slots.nc` of that case. Run `cargo xtask catalog --case 2d/slots` with the fix.

title: Turning profile offset: a steep fillet chord sends the ride far out of the bar (X354 on a 30 mm bar)

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: area:turning

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: source:agent

labels.name: P3

body:
Found during the work on #2394 (example case turning/cone-thread).

## What happens

A turned profile has a fillet that is tangent to a shoulder face. The first chords of the fillet are steep in (station, radius). The Profile Rough and Profile Finish rides go far out of the bar at the station of these chords, and come back. Each rung feeds through air.

Reading: a 30 mm bar, a collar of 30 mm diameter to Z20, a 1.2 mm fillet from the shoulder into a cone, insert `TN-1600-0R8`, stepdown 1.0, leave 0.25. The posted rough has, for each rung:

```
G00 X354.326 Z17.2
G01 X48.5 Z17.2 F0.0267
...
G01 X354.226 Z19.2 F0.05
G01 X353.936 Z19.209 F0.05
G01 X131.724 Z19.235 F0.05
G01 X87.392 Z19.278 F0.05
...
```

The rapid radius of the operation is also 177 mm, because it is the maximum radius of the outer rung. The finish ride of the same part goes out to X47.182.

The same model without the fillet (a sharp shoulder) posts a maximum of X48.6.

## Cause

`crates/motion/src/turning/offset.rs`, `profile_offset`, the closure `val`: a segment of slope `b` claims `a + b * (s - s0) + d * sqrt(1 + b * b)` at each station of its own window. That is the offset of the infinite line. For a steep, short segment the tangent point of the ball is not on the segment at these stations. The correct claim there is the circle about the nearer end point.

The first chord of the fillet has a slope of 16.6. With `d` = 10.05 the claim is 167 mm above the segment.

A vertical step is not affected: `segs` drops segments with equal stations.

## Effect

- The path is safe: the ride is too far out, never too deep.
- The program wastes time: about 300 mm of feed in air for each rung.
- On a lathe with a short X travel the limit gate refuses a legal program.
- The bisection toward the spike writes many very short moves (see the related issue about zero-length blocks).

## What is expected

The offset of a segment is limited to the stations where the tangent point is on the segment. Outside them the end point circles make the claim. The ride of a filleted shoulder stays within the nose radius plus the leave of the profile.

## Workaround

Model the shoulder as a sharp corner. The case of #2394 does this.

Refs #2394

body:
Found by the new Windows check (Windows 11, Git for Windows defaults: `core.autocrlf=true`), main 380c29b3c, `cargo xtask gate quick`.

## What happens

Git for Windows checks text files out with CRLF by default. `.gitattributes` pins `crates/app/tests/golden/**`, tester kits, examples and `*.sh` to LF, but not every fixture that tests compare byte for byte or parse. Four suites (17 tests) fail on such a checkout, each within a second:

| Suite | Reads | Pinned? |
|---|---|---|
| post `explain_fanuc_family`, `explain_remaining` | `crates/post/tests/golden/explain/*.nc` | **no** |
| app `wire_taper_angle` | `crates/app/tests/edm/wire-iso-fixture.mch` (include_str) | **no** |
| app `import_step_curve_guard` | `testdata/models/box.step` (include_str) | **no** |

Example: `fanuc_explain_golden_preserves_program` - left (generated) ends lines with `\n`, right (golden from the checkout) with `\r\n`; the content is otherwise identical.

## Fix

Pin every byte-compared or parsed text fixture to LF, e.g.:

```
crates/*/tests/golden/** text eol=lf
crates/*/tests/**/*.mch  text eol=lf
testdata/**/*.step       text eol=lf
testdata/**/*.stp        text eol=lf
```

(or one broader rule for `crates/*/tests/**` and `testdata/**`), then `git add --renormalize .`. A unit test in xtask (or a CI-free check) could assert that `git check-attr eol` is `lf` for every file under the golden/fixture dirs.

## Done means

On a fresh Windows checkout with `core.autocrlf=true`, the four suites above pass; `git check-attr eol -- <each fixture>` reports `lf`.

title: Bore: a helical strategy (continuous helix to full depth, then a floor circle)

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: claimed
labels.description: An agent is working on this - see the claim comment

labels.name: area:2d
labels.description: 2D milling

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

labels.name: P6
labels.description: Accepted enhancement, not scheduled

body:
### What are you trying to do

Counterbores for M6 cap screws in aluminium: Ø11 × 7 deep, cut with a Ø6 flat end mill on a small 3-axis mill (LinuxCNC, ER20 spindle). The usual way to cut these is helical interpolation: the tool spirals down on the wall radius to full depth, then runs one flat circle at the floor. It never plunges straight into solid material.

In 0.24.0 the Bore operation is a level-by-level ring ladder. At each step-down level the tool dives at the hole centre, sweeps out to the wall and runs a ring, then moves to the next level. The source describes the first engagement as the bore's centre dive, and the Lead-in tab has no entry choice for Bore. Linking → Level to level → Helix helps between levels, but that helix runs on a 1 mm radius at the centre and the first dive is still a plunge. With a 1 mm step-down that comes to 7 plunges and 7 rings per counterbore.

On a light machine, a flat end mill plunging into solid aluminium is the move most likely to chatter, pack chips or snap the tool. That's why the helical cycle is the default for counterbores and holes bored with an end mill.

### How you imagine it working

A **Helical** strategy in the Bore operation (or a separate Helical bore operation):

- The tool positions over the hole at the retract plane and descends on a **continuous helix** whose radius puts the cutter's rim on the finished wall (hole radius − tool radius − stock to leave), from Top Z to the hole floor.
- **Helix pitch** (mm per turn) is set by the user, with a sensible automatic value. Alternatively a maximum ramp angle.
- At the floor, **one full flat circle** to remove the ramp step, then a move off the wall towards the centre before retracting.
- Optional **spring pass**: a second floor circle with no extra depth.
- **Climb or conventional**, as Bore has now.
- For holes too wide for one helix to clear the core (wider than about 2 × tool diameter): helix at an inner radius first, then step out in rings at the floor, or simply refuse with a clear message.
- **Through holes:** continue the helix past the floor by the break-through allowance.

The rest of Bore can stay as it is (hole detection, per-hole floors, the reach checks).

Happy to test builds on the counterbore case above and air-cut the result on my machine.

Requested by @vilts (relayed by the user, 2026-11-19), after the #2603 kit ran clean in his Robodrill's Manual Guide i graphic simulation: today the simulation draws a default blank, and he does not know how to set it by hand.

## What

Manual Guide i reads a blank (stock) definition block near the top of a program and uses it in the animation. An **opt-in** Fanuc post option writes the setup's stock as that block, after the program number and before the first motion.

Codes as the user's reading of the manual summarises them (to be verified against the manual):

| Code | Blank |
|---|---|
| G1902 | rectangular block: B width (X), D depth (Y), H height (Z), I/J/K = X/Y/Z distance from the block's lowest corner to the work origin |
| G1900 | round bar (along Z) |
| G1906 | round bar along X |
| G1901 / G1907 | hollow round bar (along Z / X) |
| G1903 / G1904 | square bar / hollow square bar |

Example (100 x 60 x 30 block, G54 at the top centre): `G1902 B100. D60. H30. I50. J30. K30.`

Source (public Fanuc documentation, behaviour only): Manual Guide i milling and turning operator's manual, https://www.cnc.uk.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/04/Manual-Guide-Milling-and-Turning-Manual.pdf

## Rules

- **Off by default.** A control without Manual Guide i can alarm on G1902, so the option is per machine (a machine/post property, e.g. "Manual Guide i blank"), never on for every Fanuc output.
- Box stock -> G1902; a cylinder stock -> G1900 (or G1906 when its axis is X); any other stock shape -> no block and a comment saying why, not a wrong block.
- I/J/K come from the setup's WCS origin relative to the stock's minimum corner, in program units (G20/G21), with the signs the manual gives. A yawed or rotated WCS that the block cannot describe -> no block plus a comment.
- No other post output changes (golden files stay the same with the option off).

## Research first (agent)

Read the manual's blank-figure section and confirm: the exact address letters and signs for G1902 and G1900 (incl. the bar's length and the axis position), where in the program the block must stand (before or after G90/G54, before the first tool change), whether it needs Manual Guide i "animation" mode only, and inch behaviour. Record the answers here before code.

## Done means

- The Fanuc post has the option, off by default; with it on, a box stock and a cylinder stock each post the right block (golden tests), and an unsupported stock posts a comment, not a block.
- vilts confirms in his Manual Guide i simulation that the drawn blank matches the stock (one short kit file).

body:
**Research only.** No code until the open questions below are answered and the concrete sub-issues are filed (AGENTS.md "needs-research is research, not code").

## Where this comes from

A wire EDM user, Alex (@alextreseder; CamCraft Discord, 2026-11-19), asked whether our XYUV (+Z) path is collision-aware and handles swallowtails. His points, in short:

- The easy case: the wire (kerf) radius is smaller than every local radius of the part. Then each ruled face is offset with an arc join and projected onto the XY and UV planes.
- The hard case: the radius is not smaller than all local radii. Then the degenerate **local and global swallowtails** must be healed and sewn with a bounded-tolerance technique. In general this is one of the hardest CAD-kernel problems, but for wire EDM it splits into **two 2D problems** (the XY and UV planes), which makes it tractable.
- He has a working procedure (currently a FreeCAD macro) and offered to share it.

## What CamCraft does today (main)

- 4-axis ruled wire cut (#537): an upper and a lower closed profile, paired into rulings by normalised arc length or by sync points (`crates/motion/src/wire_edm/ruled.rs`, `pairing.rs`); per-ruling widening (#1170, `ruled_widen.rs`).
- Kerf: each profile is offset in 2D, and the rulings are laid over those parallels.
- Degenerate results are **refused, not healed**: the fold law (the ruled surface folds back between rulings) and the crossing law (the surface crosses itself at the quarter heights) in `ruled_laws.rs`, plus the kerf and gouge laws, run before the path leaves the generator.

So the easy case works, and the hard case gives a refusal with a reason. Healing is the gap.

## Open questions

1. Which swallowtail cases occur in practice for XYUV: local (one corner tighter than the kerf radius) and global (two distant parts of a profile approach each other), on the XY plane, the UV plane, or both, and when the two planes disagree?
2. What is the healing procedure? Trim the self-intersections of each 2D offset (published offset-curve methods), then re-pair the rulings? How is the pairing kept consistent when one plane loses a loop the other plane keeps?
3. What tolerance bounds the healing, and how is the result checked (the fold and crossing laws must still pass on the healed surface)?
4. When healing changes the cut part (a corner the wire cannot reach), how is that shown to the user: the existing uncut-corner note, or a refusal when the change is above a tolerance?
5. Which of today's refusals would become healed results, and which must stay refusals (Prime Directive: correct or visibly refused)?

## What would help (from Alex or anyone)

- A **written description** of the procedure: steps, tolerances, how local vs. global swallowtails are sewn.
- If the macro itself is shared: its **licence**. We can reuse code only under a licence compatible with this project (MIT or Apache-2.0); otherwise we implement from the description and from published literature.
- **Test shapes** that make local and global swallowtails (simple STEP or DXF profiles, upper and lower). These become test fixtures for the fold and crossing laws even before any healing exists.

Clean-room: published literature, the contributor's own description, and our own design notes only; no material from Autodesk products.

## Done means

The questions above are answered in comments, and the concrete sub-issues are filed (each with one P*, one effort label, area labels, a Done-means line and "Part of #this"); then this umbrella is closed.

## What the user wants

1. Type a text string, for example a part number `SN-0471`.
2. Pick the face to engrave and place the text on that face.
3. Set the text height and the tool.
4. CamCraft makes the engraving toolpath, verifies it and posts it.

## What exists today

- `OpType::Engrave` and `OpType::Trace` machine 2D geometry along the tool centreline. They obey the mark law (#1595): a shallow mark passes, a deep cut is refused.
- 2D geometry comes from a DXF sketch (the `Sketch` entity, #1862). Work to feed sketch chains to Engrave and Trace is #1869. SVG import is #1880.
- There is no way to make geometry by typing text. A user today must draw the letters in a CAD program, export a DXF, and import it.

## What to build

- A text-to-outline step: convert the typed string into glyph outlines as 2D regions (outer loop + hole loops for letters such as A, B, O). Use one of the fonts already bundled in `assets/ui/fonts/`; the outlines are the same vectors the UI draws. Flatten the glyph curves to polylines within the setup tolerance. Clean-room: only the font's own licensed outlines, no vendor letter shapes.
- An undoable command (for example `InsertText`): the text string, height, and the placement become a `Sketch` the operation kinds already read. Ship its MCP tool with it (#128 law).
- Placement: select a planar face (or the setup top plane) in the viewport, then set X/Y and rotation. The existing `sketch::face_frame` code gives the face frame.
- Parameters on the Engrave operation: text string, height (mm or inch through the unit lens), letter spacing, depth (bounded by the mark law), tool, feed, and climb. The toolpath path is the existing Engrave/Trace generator.
- Two ride modes later, both from the same outlines: ride the glyph boundary with a small end mill or v-bit, and single-line engraving on the glyph skeleton with a v-bit. Pick one for the first cut; record the choice in `docs/decisions/`.

## Suggested label triage

`enhancement`, `area:2d`, `P6`, `effort:high` (safety floor: new toolpath and posted G-code). The filing account has no label rights; a collaborator sets these.

## Done means

The user types a string, picks a face and a spot, sets a height and a tool, and CamCraft generates, verifies and posts an engraving toolpath. A golden test pins the CL output for a known string and font. The placement, `.camproj` round-trip and MCP tests pass.

The maintainer asked for this work, in his own words (2026-11-18):

> issue; p4; there is shaded and wireframe today. There should be a shaded with no edges, and wireframe "see thru" as well.

## State of the code

The Browser pane has a "Solids" choice with two modes (`DisplayMode` in `crates/ui/src/state.rs`, radios in `crates/ui/src/egui_app/browser_pane.rs`):

- `ShadedEdges`: flat-shaded faces with the CAD wire over them. It is the default.
- `Wireframe`: faces go to the depth buffer only, so the model reads as a hidden-line drawing. Hidden edges do not show.

## Wanted

Four display modes:

1. **Shaded** (with edges). The current default. No change.
2. **Shaded, no edges.** Faces only. No CAD wire over them. Edges of a picked or hovered feature still show, so that picking stays visible.
3. **Wireframe** (hidden lines removed). The current mode. No change.
4. **Wireframe, see-through.** Every edge draws, front and back, with no hidden-line removal. The model does not hide the stock, the fixtures or the toolpath behind it. Hidden edges may draw in a lighter tone, so the front stays readable.

Details:
- The choice stays one control in the Browser pane. Four radios or one drop-down. Plain English labels: "Shaded", "Shaded, no edges", "Wireframe", "Wireframe, see-through". Tooltips say what each does.
- The mode is view state (a direct field flip, never a command), as today. It applies to the model, the stock and the fixtures in the same way. The toolpath and the simulation stock follow their own rules and stay readable in each mode.
- The setting is saved with the other view settings, if the others are saved. An old file without the field loads with the default.
- Picking works in each mode. In "Wireframe, see-through" a click picks the edge nearest to the cursor, front or back, with the nearest to the camera first. State the rule in the test.
- The renderer builds the edge and face passes once for each geometry change (precalculate and cache; frame target under 10 ms). No per-frame rebuild of the edge lists.

## Constraints

- A UI PR needs before and after screenshots of all four modes in the PR body. Tests assert labels, roles, which mode is selected, the state field and the picking rule. They do not assert pixels. Pixel snapshots are release-lane only and a PR never changes a PNG.
- Update the layout test of the Browser page. Keep each file under about 400 lines.
- `DisplayMode` is also used by the wasm build. The new modes must work there.

## Done means

- A test shows that each radio sets its mode and that the labels exist.
- A test shows the draw list for each mode: faces and edges as listed above.
- A test shows picking in "Wireframe, see-through" with the stated rule.
- The PR has the screenshots.

> bug; tools like plasma cutter - or laser for that matter, and prob waterjet as well. Would require piercing and dwell data.. Lasers usually have 1-4 piercing steps that can be used all or just one. just to get thru different thickness of material. Same with plasma.. piercing height, power at height, pressure of gas, movement of torch/laser head etc etc. Use perplexit to research this in a subagent and make a issue ticket from it where this types of tools getter better coverage.

(Maintainer, 2026-11-13, in chat.)

## What exists today

- Plasma only. `ToolKind::Torch` (`crates/tools/src/tools.rs`) is a kerf width plus rpm 0; it carries no cutting data. I found no laser or waterjet tool kind in `tools.rs`.
- The plasma operation (`crates/motion/src/plasma/mod.rs`, `emit.rs`; app side `crates/app/src/operation/types/plasma.rs`, `crates/app/src/project/plasma_dto.rs`; page `crates/ui/src/egui_app/plasma_page.rs`) has three optional per-operation numbers: pierce height, cut height, pierce delay. Left empty means "set by the controller" (AutoFS).
- The Tormach plasma post (`assets/posts/tormach-plasma.cps`) writes M207/M208/M209 for those three values and G16 for the pierce, and leaves volts, amps and gas to the control's own table. Nothing else (power, gas, pressure, torch motion at the pierce) can be stated anywhere.
- Related open issues: 621 (plasma research umbrella), 1447 (common-line cutting and marking), 1452 (DXF import for 2D cuts). No open issue covers pierce data; a "pierce" search finds only closed plasma work (670, 671).

## What is missing

1. Cut data lives on the operation, not on the tool, and is not keyed by material or thickness. Changing plate thickness means re-typing numbers.
2. Only one pierce, with one height and one delay. No transfer height, no puddle-jump (lift after pierce), no creep or start-speed ramp on exit, no amperage or gas on the tool.
3. Laser and waterjet have no tool kind, so there is nowhere to put multi-stage pierce data.
4. Posts have no way to say "this stage cannot be written in this dialect".

## Research summary (facts and concepts only, own words)

Plasma
- Transfer height: the low height where the arc first transfers to the plate. Pierce height: the higher height held while the arc pierces (limits spray onto the torch). Pierce delay: time held after transfer before the head moves. Cut height: stand-off while cutting. Torch height control holds a target arc voltage as a stand-in for the distance during the cut.
- Puddle jump (optional): after the pierce, lift to a percentage of pierce height for a short dwell to clear molten metal, then drop to cut height.
- Each system and consumable set has a maximum pierce thickness; thicker plate needs an edge start (the arc begins off the plate edge). Kerf comes from the cut chart.
- The maker's cut chart is the source of values (current, gas type and pressure, heights, voltage, speed). It normally sits in the control's material table; the program selects it and may override single values.

Laser
- Makers document up to four sequential pierce stages, each with its own time, power, pulse frequency, duty cycle, focus, nozzle distance, gas type and pressure; a stage with zero time is skipped. Parameters may ramp from a start to an end value inside a stage.
- Pierce kinds named by makers: ramped, pulsed (gradual), and a forceful short pierce; definitions vary by machine, so the data model must not hard-code them.
- Cooling dwell or gas blow is machine-specific; no standard length exists.
- Normal practice: the technology table (material and thickness) holds the recipe, the NC program selects the table and pierce type and may override.

Waterjet
- Methods: stationary, dynamic (moving toward the path while piercing), wiggle or circular (short oscillation), and low-pressure or pressure-ramp pierce for brittle or laminated material (glass, stone, ceramic, composites). Abrasive can be delayed after water starts, or fed first with pressure ramped up from low.
- No universal pierce time by thickness exists; it depends on material, pressure, nozzle and method, so it must be the user's value.

Control table versus program: recipes are usually in the control's table (selected by material and thickness) with the program choosing and sometimes overriding. A CAM system therefore needs both: store the recipe, then either post the selector or post explicit values, by dialect.

## Proposed data model

A cut-data record per tool, keyed by material and thickness (rows the user adds, copies and deletes):

- Cut parameters: cut height, feed, kerf; for plasma amperage, gas type and pressure, arc voltage; for laser power, frequency, duty, gas type and pressure, nozzle distance, focus; for waterjet pressure and abrasive flow.
- Pierce: an ordered list of 0 to 4 stages, every stage optional and individually enableable. Each stage has height, duration (dwell), power or pressure, frequency and duty (laser), gas and pressure, an optional ramp end value, and head motion during the pierce (none, wiggle or circular amplitude, or moving toward the path). Plasma uses one stage plus optional transfer height and puddle-jump (percent and dwell). Waterjet adds method, low-pressure value and abrasive delay.
- Pierce capacity per record: maximum pierceable thickness, and whether an edge start is allowed.
- Every number is entered by the user or copied from the maker's chart. Shipped example rows are marked "example" in the file and in the UI.

Editing: a cut-data table on the tool page (undoable commands, an MCP tool and script verb per the command law). The operation chooses a row (or "none: the machine's own table") and may override single values; overrides are commands too.

Operation behaviour: pierce at the start of the lead-in, run the stages in order (height move, dwell and head motion per stage), then the cut-height move and lead-in. The generated path carries the stages as records in the CL file so the post and the verifier read the same data.

Posts: each dialect writes the stages it can (dwell, height moves, selector codes or direct values). A stage or value the dialect cannot express makes the post refuse with a named reason, or write a visible comment line naming what was left to the control; it is never dropped silently. The Tormach post keeps M207/M208/M209 for the plasma values and refuses a multi-stage laser record.

## Safety rules

- A thickness above the tool's pierce capacity is refused, unless the operation states an edge start (then the lead-in must start off the plate, and that is verified).
- No silent default for a pierce time or height: an empty value either posts "controller's table" as an explicit, commented choice on a dialect that has one, or refuses.
- Stage values are checked at command creation (non-negative times and heights, power within 0 to 100 percent, at most four stages).
- Values are the user's and the machine maker's; shipped examples are labelled as examples and nothing was run on a real machine. Verification (stage order, pierce inside a kept part, head motion hitting a neighbour) joins the existing plasma laws.
- This changes posted output, so it is at least effort:high.

## Suggested slices

1. Tool-side cut-data record for the existing plasma torch (material and thickness rows, transfer height, puddle jump, pierce capacity), project file round-trip, undoable commands, MCP tool. The operation picks a row.
2. Plasma generation and the Tormach post use the row; refusal for thickness above capacity and the edge-start rule; laws and goldens.
3. Laser tool kind and machine kind with 1 to 4 pierce stages; CL records and a first laser post (dwell and height moves, explicit comment lines).
4. Waterjet tool kind: pierce methods, low-pressure pierce, abrasive delay; post support.
5. Docs and shipped example rows.

Slices 3 and 4 may need their own research issues for machine kinds; file them when slice 1 lands.

Done means: a plasma, laser or waterjet tool carries material and thickness keyed cut data with up to four ordered optional pierce stages; the operation uses the chosen row at the lead-in start; each post writes every stage or refuses or comments what it cannot; a too-thick plate without an edge start is refused; tests pin all of these.

Related: 621, 1447, 1452, 670, 671.

body:
Asked for by the maintainer (2026-11-13, in chat), after a feature comparison with the open-source project stevecad/camlib: "We wanna cover some of the toolpaths and things like that at first." and, on the suggested picks: "Lets create issues on your suggestions, they made sense." On sources: "We should use perplexity to find literature on those types of toolpaths and not copy them straight up".

What is missing: there is no V-carve operation. The engrave ride follows a line at one depth; it does not set depth from the width of the region.

Wanted: a 2D operation "V-carve" for V-bits (included angle from the tool). For closed regions (text, signs, inlays) the tool centre follows the medial axis and the depth at each point is the one where the cone touches both walls, limited by a maximum depth. Where the region is wider than the cone reaches at maximum depth, an optional flat-clearing pass (same or a second flat tool) removes the floor. Parameters are user choices with defaults: max depth, flat clearing on/off and its tool, start depth, stepdown for deep carves.

Safety: the cone must never cut outside the selected region at any depth (pinned by a test that sweeps the cone along the path against the region outline). A tool that is not a V-bit, an open region, or a tip flat larger than the narrowest feature is refused by name. Undoable command, MCP tool, simulation and collision checks like any 2D op.

Sources: step one of the work is a literature search (Perplexity) for published papers and handbooks on medial-axis / Voronoi-based V-carving; the algorithm is written from those and named in the module provenance comment. camlib is a feature list only: no code is copied or adapted from it.

Done means: a V-carve op on a closed text outline generates, simulates without leaving the region, posts through the existing posts, has a golden CL file and an MCP tool; fuzzed degenerate regions (self-intersecting, zero-width) give a clean error; the literature used is cited in the PR and the provenance comment.

body:
Found while working #984.

**What happens:** the same commit plans the same part differently on two platforms. `app pocket3d_hsm::the_users_bore_roughs_adaptive_level_by_level_and_verifies_clean` (release) on ecb54b7f:

| platform | rings levels | moves / planar / arcs |
|---|---|---|
| Windows (the #850 measure, PR #865) | Z 20.000 | 5530 / 5497 / 600 |
| macOS, Apple silicon (Homebrew rustc 1.99.1) | Z 20.000 (crossing at -2.33, -2.78) | 5786 / 5753 / 651 |

macOS is deterministic run to run, so it is not hash-map order. Rust does not contract `a*b+c` into FMA unless asked, so the most likely cause is the platform libm: `f64::sin`, `cos`, `atan2`, `hypot`, `exp`, `powf` call the system math library (MSVC CRT, glibc, Apple libm), which are not correctly rounded and differ in the last place. The STEP tessellation and the adaptive planner both use them, and the planner's crossing and acceptance tests are knife edges a 16 nm change flips (#882, #982). Not yet confirmed which call sites diverge, and not run on Linux.

**Why it matters:** a toolpath (and so the posted G-code) for the same part, tool and parameters depends on the OS the user runs. Every output is still verified and a crossing plan is refused by name, so this is not a gouge; but golden counts and exact plan pins cannot hold across platforms, and a user can see a different path from the same project file on two machines.

**Possible directions (open):** route the geometry and planner transcendental calls through a pure-Rust deterministic libm (the `libm` crate is already in Cargo.lock) so every platform rounds the same; or make the planner's decisions robust to sub-micron perturbation (#882, #982). Either changes toolpaths and needs every adaptive fixture re-measured.

Done means: the cause is confirmed on a second platform (Windows or Linux run of the bore test, plus which calls diverge), and either the output is made platform-identical with goldens re-measured, or the decision not to is recorded.

Refs #984, #882, #982.

body:
**Subscribe to this issue** (the "Subscribe" button on the right) if you work from a fork of CamCraft, especially with an AI agent.

Forks sync product code only at release tags (AGENTS.md "A fork syncs from upstream at each cut tag"). But the *process* - `AGENTS.md`, the agent definitions in `.claude/agents/`, the skills in `.claude/skills/` and `scripts/gate.*` - changes between releases, and a fork's agents should follow the current rules (review labels, priority labels, release steps, and so on).

**How it works:**
- `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` holds one number. Every PR that changes a process file bumps it.
- Every such PR also adds a comment **here**: the new version, what changed, and what to pull. Subscribers get one notification per change.
- A fork's agent compares its `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` with upstream's at the start of each session and, if upstream is newer, pulls just the process files (AGENTS.md "Process files sync on every session"). Product code still waits for the next release tag.

**To pull by hand:**
```
git fetch upstream
git checkout upstream/main -- AGENTS.md .claude/agents .claude/skills .claude/PROCESS_VERSION scripts/gate.ps1 scripts/gate.sh
git commit -m "chore(process): sync process files to upstream PROCESS_VERSION <n>"
```

This issue stays open and pinned. It's labelled `P?` so no agent ever picks it up as work.
